title: John of Damascus and the icons
hookLine: he defends images: God became visible, so he can be pictured

cards: A story is told of soldiers on a ladder at a palace gate, pulling down a picture of Christ.
Across an empire, painted images are being taken out of churches, plastered over, broken; the emperor's party says pictures of holy things are idols, and must go.

Far away, in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, a monk named John, from a family that served in Damascus, picks up his pen to argue for the pictures. His argument doesn't start with art.
It starts with Christmas. Today's word is icon.

teach.b: Icon comes from the Greek word for image, eikon. The letter to the Colossians uses it about Christ himself; in the Douay-Rheims it calls him "the image of the invisible God." That's John's starting point.
In the old law, God gave no shape to look at, so nobody could paint him.

teach.h: GOD WAS SEEN, SO HE CAN BE SHOWN.
teach.b: But now, John says, God has been seen. He was born, he had a face, he ate and walked and was touched. So a painter of Christ isn't inventing the invisible God out of his own head.
John's best-known line runs, roughly: I do not worship matter; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake, and through matter worked my salvation.
Wood, paint, bread, water, a body: God used stuff, so stuff can be honored. Then a careful distinction. Worship belongs to God alone.
An icon receives honor, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love, and, borrowing a line from Basil the Great, John says the honor passes through the picture to the person it shows.
Later, a council of bishops at Nicaea agreed and approved the honoring of images. Catholics and Orthodox Christians both honor John as a saint, and Catholics call him a Doctor of the Church.
Some people describe an icon this way: a window, not a wall. Something to look through, not to stop at.

how: In Catholic and Orthodox churches people light candles before icons, bow, or kiss them, honoring the person shown; the Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint John Damascene as a Doctor of the Church.

o: a sacred statue worshiped in God's place
a holy image honored for the one it shows
a small charm kept for luck or protection

games.q: you're John. the emperor's party says every holy picture is an idol. how do you begin your defense?
o: argue that the pictures are beautiful art.
start with God becoming visible in Christ.
say people will be upset if the pictures go.
games.why: John starts with the Incarnation: God was seen, so what was seen can be painted, and the honor passes to the one shown.

practice: If you have an icon or a holy card nearby, use it; if not, glance at one on a screen, then set the screen face down and hold the image in your mind.
Look first at the eyes, then the hands, and let your gaze rest without analyzing, breathing slowly. If you pray, let the image carry your prayer past it.

wordCard.voice: Icon. From the Greek for image: a holy picture that, for those who honor it, points past itself to the one it shows. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: image, likeness — the word Colossians uses for Christ, and the root of icon.

carryVoice: Your line: a window, not a wall. A picture can point past itself. Until tomorrow.
